question: What leads the new king to oppress the Israelites, and what measures does he take one after another?
The verb יָרֵא (yare, “fear”) explains the midwives' attitude: how does the fear of God lead them to disobey the king, and what does God do for them?
What words of the chapter echo the blessing of Genesis 1 and the promises to Abraham, and why does Pharaoh see them as a threat?
Shiphrah and Puah, two women without power, resist an unjust order: in the face of what order or pressure would you need their courage?
Which people act to save the baby, and what does each of them do?
What does Moses' attempt to take justice into his own hands reveal about him, and why does it end in flight?
The verb זָכַר (zakhar, “remember”) appears in verse 24 together with “heard,” “looked” and “took notice”: what does this sequence of verbs say about God's response to the cry?
Moses names his son Gershom, saying “I have become a foreigner in a foreign land”: in what place or stage of life do you also feel like a foreigner?
What catches Moses' attention on the mountain, and what gestures does God ask of him as he approaches?
What verbs does God use to describe what He has seen, heard and known, and what is Moses' role in what He has decided to do?

In verse 14 God introduces Himself with the verb הָיָה (hayah, “be”), in the form אֶהְיֶה (ehyeh, “I am” or “I will be”): how does this name connect to the promise “I will surely be with you” in verse 12?
“Who am I?”: in what task do you feel too small, and what changes when God's answer is “I will be with you”?
What three signs does God give Moses, and what are they for?

The verb חָזַק (chazaq, “harden, strengthen”) appears in the announcement that Pharaoh's heart will be hardened: how do you understand this expression, which returns many times in the following chapters?
What objections does Moses raise, and why does the last one provoke the LORD's anger?
“What is that in your hand?”: what simple resource of your life could God use in a way you cannot imagine?
What new order does Pharaoh give the taskmasters, and how does it affect the Israelites' work?
Pharaoh calls the people “lazy,” with the verb רָפָה (rafah, “be slack, idle”): how does he use this accusation to reject the request to worship?
What does Pharaoh's question “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice?” reveal, and how will the rest of the book answer it?
Moses complains to God that everything got worse after he obeyed: how do you deal with obedience that at first seems to bring only trouble?
How many actions does the LORD promise to do for the people in verses 6 to 8, and with what phrase do they begin and end?
The verb גָּאַל (gaal, “redeem”) is the same as the “kinsman-redeemer” of Ruth: what idea of kinship and responsibility does it bring to the deliverance from Egypt?
Why can't the people listen to Moses, and what does the expression “uncircumcised lips” reveal about how Moses sees himself?
The people do not listen “because of their broken spirit”: when have weariness or pain kept you from hearing good news?
What happens when Aaron throws down his staff before Pharaoh, and how do the sorcerers respond?
The word לֵב (lev, “heart”) is tied to Pharaoh throughout the chapter: what different forms does the text use to speak of his heart, and who is the subject of each one?
What does God want the Egyptians and Pharaoh to “know” through the signs, according to verses 5 and 17?
Pharaoh “did not take even this to heart”: what sign in your life have you preferred not to take seriously?
What does Pharaoh promise when the frogs trouble him, and what does he do when he gets relief?
The magicians admit: “This is the finger of God,” with the word אֶצְבַּע (etsba, “finger”): what does this expression acknowledge, and why does Pharaoh still not give in?
What is new in the plague of flies with the setting apart of the land of Goshen, and what is it meant to show?
Pharaoh offers half-concessions: “sacrifice within this land,” “you must not go very far”: where do you also try to obey only halfway?
What warning comes before the hail, and how do Pharaoh's servants react in different ways?
What reasons does God give Pharaoh for not having destroyed him at once, according to verses 14 to 16?
Pharaoh confesses that “the LORD is righteous,” using צַדִּיק (tsaddiq, “righteous”): why does this confession not change his behavior (v. 34)?
Pharaoh sins again as soon as the threat passes: how do you react after a crisis that made you seek God is over?
Whom does Pharaoh agree to let go in the negotiation, and who does Moses insist must go?
The verb עָנָה (anah, “humble oneself”) is in the question “How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me?”: what does the refusal to humble himself cost Pharaoh and Egypt?
According to verses 1 and 2, why should these stories be told to children and grandchildren?
What story of God's action in your life would you like to tell the next generations?
What does Moses announce about midnight, and how far will the last plague reach, according to verse 5?
The word בְּכוֹר (bekhor, “firstborn”) dominates verse 5: how is this last plague linked to what God said in 4:22-23 about Israel being His “firstborn”?
Why does the text point out that the people find favor in the eyes of the Egyptians and that Moses is highly regarded among them?
This is one of the hardest chapters of the book: how do you deal, in faith, with texts in which God's judgment also strikes the innocent?
How must the lamb be chosen, prepared and eaten, and in what clothes must the people eat it?
The verb פָּסַח (pasach, “pass over, spare”) gives the Passover its name: what does the sign of the blood on the doors mean in verses 13 and 23?
Why does the text foresee the children's question, “What does this service mean to you?”, and what does the answer teach about the memory of faith?
A “mixed multitude” leaves with Israel, and there is one law for the native and the foreigner: what does this say about who can belong to God's people?
Why doesn't God lead the people by the shortest route, and how does He guide them by day and by night?
The verb פָּדָה (padah, “redeem”) is used for the firstborn: why must Israel redeem every firstborn, and what memory does this gesture carry?
What does the command that the deliverance be “a sign on your hand” and “a reminder on your forehead” mean?
God spares the people a war they were not yet ready for: what longer road might you be walking because of God's care?
How do the people react when they see the Egyptians approaching, and of what do they accuse Moses?
Moses says “see the LORD's salvation,” using יְשׁוּעָה (yeshuah, “salvation”): what must the people do and what must they only watch, according to verses 13 and 14?
How do the command “be still” (v. 14) and the command “go forward” (v. 15) fit together?
“The LORD will fight for you”: in what current battle do you need to stop fighting alone and trust?
What images does the song use to describe the LORD and what He did at the sea?
The chapter ends with the LORD saying “I am the LORD who heals you,” using רָפָא (rafa, “heal”): how is this promise linked to the episode of the bitter waters of Marah?
What does it show that the people, three days after singing, are already grumbling at Marah?
Miriam leads the women with tambourines and dancing: in what way do you celebrate what God does in your life?
What rules does Moses give for gathering the manna, and what happens to those who keep some for the next day?
The name מָן (man, “manna”) echoes the question of verse 15, “What is it?”: what does it mean for the people to be fed by something they could not even name?
How does the manna become, according to verses 4 and 22 to 30, a test and a school for learning the Sabbath rest?
“Whoever gathered much had no excess, and whoever gathered little had no shortfall”: what does this measure teach about the way you accumulate and share?
Why do the people quarrel with Moses at Rephidim, and how does God provide water?
The verb נָסָה (nasah, “test”) appears in the question “Is the LORD among us or not?”: what does it mean to put God to the test in this sense?
What does the scene of Moses' raised hands, held up by Aaron and Hur, suggest about the relationship between prayer and struggle?
Moses needed others to hold up his tired hands: who holds you up today, and whom could you hold up?
What does Jethro observe in Moses' routine, and why does he say “What you are doing is not good”?
The verb שָׁפַט (shafat, “judge”) describes Moses' work and then that of the chosen leaders: what qualities does verse 21 require of those who will judge the people?
What leads Jethro, a priest of Midian, to bless the LORD and offer sacrifices, and what does this say about outsiders who recognize God's work?
What load are you trying to carry alone, and who could share it with you?
What preparations must the people make before the third day, and what limits are set around the mountain?
The word סְגֻלָּה (segullah, “treasured possession”) describes Israel in verse 5: how is this choice linked to the phrase “the whole earth is Mine” and to the mission of being “a kingdom of priests”?
What image does God use in verse 4 to sum up the exodus from Egypt, and what does it communicate about the purpose of the deliverance?
Before thunder, fire and the trumpet, the people tremble: how does the sense of God's greatness coexist with His nearness in your faith?
Which commandments deal with the relationship with God and which with the relationship with one's neighbor?
Why do the commandments begin by recalling “who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” before any command?
The verb חָמַד (chamad, “covet”) closes the list of commandments: what is different about a commandment that deals with inner desire, and not only with acts?
The commandment of rest includes servants, animals and foreigners: how do you practice rest and allow it to those who depend on you?
What limits does the law set on the servitude of a Hebrew, and what protections does it give to a woman sold as a servant?
The word חׇפְשִׁי (chofshi, “free”) appears at the beginning and end of the laws on servants: in what situations must the servant go free, and what does this reveal about the purpose of these laws?
Did the principle “eye for eye, tooth for tooth” serve to increase or to limit revenge, and how have Jews and Christians interpreted it?
The law orders the release of a servant injured by his own master: how can ancient laws help you think about the dignity of those who work under others' authority today?
What kinds of damage and loss are dealt with in verses 1 to 15, and what is the law's most common answer?
The word גֵּר (ger, “foreigner”) comes with a reason: “for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt”: how should the memory of suffering shape the way we treat the vulnerable?
Why does God say He will hear the cry of the widow, the orphan and the poor, and what link is there between the returned cloak and “I am gracious” in verse 27?
What economic practices of your daily life could be reviewed in light of the ban on exploiting the poor who borrow?
What attitudes does the text forbid in court and in disputes, and who is protected in these verses?
The word שֹׁחַד (shochad, “bribe”) comes with an explanation: “a bribe blinds those who see”: in what way can self-interest blind someone's judgment?
Why does the law command helping precisely the enemy's animal, and what does this teach about our relationship with those who hate us?
“Do not follow the crowd in wrongdoing”: in what situation do you feel the pressure of the majority against what is right?
What steps make up the ceremony confirming the covenant, and what do the people answer twice?
The expressions “Book of the Covenant” and “blood of the covenant” use בְּרִית (berit, “covenant”): what might the blood shared between the altar and the people symbolize?
What does it mean that the elders “saw God, and they ate and drank,” without being harmed?
Moses waits six days in the cloud before being called: how do you deal with times of waiting in your life of faith?
How are the ark, the mercy seat and the cherubim described, and where does God say He will speak with Moses?
The verb שָׁכַן (shakan, “dwell”) appears in verse 8: what does it mean that the sanctuary is built so that God may “dwell among them”?
Why must the offering for the sanctuary come only from those whose heart moves them to give?
Moses must make everything “according to the pattern”: in what area of your life do you need to follow a pattern you received instead of improvising?
How many layers of curtains and coverings make up the tabernacle, and what materials is each one made of?
The word מִשְׁכָּן (mishkan, “tabernacle, dwelling”) comes from the verb “dwell” of 25:8: what changes in thinking of the tabernacle as God's “dwelling” among the people?
What is the function of the veil, and what does the separation between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place communicate about God's holiness?
The tabernacle was a tent made to be taken down and carried along the way: what does this suggest about a God who goes with His people on the move?
How is the altar of burnt offering made, and what material are its parts made of?
What does the description of the courtyard, with its curtains and a single entrance, suggest about the way to approach God?
The word תָּמִיד (tamid, “continually”) describes the lamps that must burn: why could the light in the tabernacle not go out, and who was responsible for it?
The people bring the oil and the priests tend the lamps every evening: what small daily tasks keep your life of faith burning?
Where are the names of the sons of Israel engraved on Aaron's garments, and how many times do they appear?

The word זִכָּרוֹן (zikkaron, “memorial”) explains why Aaron carries the names on his shoulders and over his heart: what does it mean for the priest to present the people “as a memorial” before the LORD?
What does the inscription “HOLY TO THE LORD” on Aaron's forehead mean, and why will he “bear the iniquity of the holy things”?
Aaron carries the people's names over his heart: what names do you carry before God in prayer?
What steps make up the consecration of Aaron and his sons, from the washing to the anointing?
What might the blood placed on the ear, the thumb and the big toe of the priests signify?
The chapter ends with the verb שָׁכַן (shakan, “dwell”) twice: how do verses 45 and 46 link the exodus from Egypt to God's desire to dwell among the people?
The regular burnt offering was made morning and evening: what daily rhythm do you have for meeting with God?
How much must each person counted give as a ransom, and what does verse 15 say about the rich and the poor?
The verb כָּפַר (kafar, “make atonement”) appears with the altar of incense and the ransom money: what idea of covering or reconciliation does it bring in these verses?
Why must the priests wash their hands and feet before entering the tabernacle or approaching the altar?
Everyone pays the same half shekel, “the rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less”: what does this say about the worth of each person before God?
Whom does God call by name to carry out the work of the tabernacle, and with what gifts does He equip them?
The word חׇכְמָה (chokhmah, “wisdom”) is used here for a craftsman's skill: what does it mean that the Bible calls the talent for working gold, stone and wood wisdom?
Why, right after the instructions about the work, does the text insist that the Sabbath be kept, and of what is it a “sign”?
Bezalel is filled “with the Spirit of God” for manual work: how do you see God's presence in your daily work?
Why do the people ask Aaron for gods, and how does he lead the making of the calf and the feast?
The golden עֵגֶל (egel, “calf”) is called “your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt”: what does this phrase reveal about the people's confusion between God and an image?
What arguments does Moses use when interceding for the people, and what does the text mean by “the LORD relented from the calamity”?
Aaron says he threw the gold into the fire “and out came this calf”: in what way have you also played down your responsibility for a mistake?
What was the tent Moses pitched outside the camp like, and what happened when he went into it?
The word פָּנִים (panim, “face”) runs through the chapter: how do we reconcile “face to face” (v. 11) with “you cannot see My face” (v. 20)?
Why does Moses say he does not want to go on without God's presence, even with the promise of the land and of an angel?
Moses asks “Please show me Your glory”: what do you most want to know of God right now?
What does Moses take up the mountain, and with what words does the LORD proclaim His name?
The word חֶסֶד (chesed, “loving devotion, mercy”) appears twice in the proclamation of the name: how does it coexist, in the same text, with the justice that does not leave the guilty unpunished?
Why does Moses' face shine, and why does he wear a veil before the people?
“Slow to anger”: what would your life be like if you imitated this trait of God with the people close to you?
Who brings offerings for the tabernacle, and what does the text repeat about the disposition of the heart of those who bring them?
The word נָדִיב (nadiv, “willing, generous”) describes who should bring the offering: why is God's work built with free gifts and not with a tax?
What does the text highlight by mentioning the “skilled women” who spun with their own hands?
“Everyone whose heart stirred him”: what has your heart been asking you to offer, and what keeps you from it?
What do the craftsmen tell Moses, and what unusual order does he have to give the people?
The verb יָתַר (yatar, “be more than enough”) closes verse 7: what does it mean that the people's generosity had to be restrained, a few chapters after the golden calf?
What link does the text draw between the wisdom given by the LORD and the heart that “stirred” each person to come to the work?
In what situation have you seen, or would you like to see, a community give more than was needed for a good work?
How does Bezalel make the ark and the mercy seat, and how does this description resemble that of chapter 25?
The כַּפֹּרֶת (kapporet, “mercy seat, atonement cover”) comes from the same root as “make atonement”: what does it suggest that the place where God speaks to the people is called this?
Why does the book repeat almost word for word the instructions of chapters 25 to 30, now as work carried out?
The lampstand is made of a single piece of gold, “hammered out”: what patient and careful work might God be doing in you?
What amounts of gold, silver and bronze does the text record, and where did the silver come from?
The bronze basin is made from the מַרְאָה (marah, “mirrors”) of the women who served at the entrance of the tabernacle: what does this detail reveal about who contributed to the work?
Why does the text make a point of giving such a detailed account of the materials used?
The work is counted and recorded transparently: how do you account for what has been entrusted to you?
What do the people bring to Moses when the work is finished, and what does Moses do when he sees it completed?
The chapter ends with the verb בָּרַךְ (barakh, “bless”): what echoes of creation, when God saw His work and blessed it, do you notice in verses 32 and 43?
The phrase “just as the LORD had commanded Moses” is repeated several times: what does this repetition mean to highlight?
Moses blesses those who worked: in what way do you acknowledge and thank others for their work?
On what day is the tabernacle set up, and in what order does Moses put each piece in place?
The כָּבוֹד (kavod, “glory”) of the LORD fills the tabernacle: why can not even Moses enter, and what change does this mark since the sin of the calf?
How does the end of the book link God's presence in the tabernacle to the people's journey through the wilderness?
The people set out only when the cloud is lifted: how do you discern the time to wait and the time to move on?
